Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson at a rally in Surrey on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026. Lorne Doerkson has been sent back to Victoria for the third time by the voters of the Cariboo-Chilcotin, this time as premier of the entire province. Based on preliminary polls Doerkson, the incumbent MLA for the Conservative Party of B.C., has won 76.9 per cent of the vote as of 10:30 p.m., with 75 of 89 ballot boxes counted. His rivals, Kathryn Askew of the BC NDP, secured roughly 17.1 per cent of the vote, while Douglas Gook of the Green Party of B.C. brought home six per cent of the vote. As of Saturday, Oct. 24 at 9 p.m., the Conservative Party of B.C. is on track to form a majority government. This means that, if Doerkson’s interim-leader status is formalized, he will be B.C.’s next premier. Projections currently predict a 64-seat majority government for the Conservatives, with the NDP set to form the opposition with 27 seats. Speaking to a crowd of supporters Saturday night in Victoria, Doerkson was visibly excited and emotional. In his speech, he praised the volunteers who made this victory possible, both provincially and here in the Cariboo-Chilcotin. “To our volunteers, you knocked on doors, rain and shine, you did so much incredible work. You put up signs, you made the calls, none of this would have been possible without your hard work,” Doerkson said. “To everyone who voted tonight, including those who voted for someone else, thank you so very much. “I also want to thank my team at home, because they have done an unbelievable job. I will say this, Cariboo-Chilcotin is amazing!” During his speech, Doerkson mentioned the Cariboo several times when outlining his vision for B.C.’s future. 1a2abfe921b2de6235b0b7bf6f6b14ac.text: Doerkson set to become B.C. premier after projected Conservative majority win | Williams Lake Tribune Doerkson set to become B.C. premier after projected Conservative majority win Lorne Doerkson takes the stage as the B.C. Conservatives are the projected 2026 election winners by majority. Lorne Doerkson is poised to become British Columbia’s next premier after leading the Conservative Party to a projected majority government Saturday, Oct. 24, barely five weeks after taking over a party struggling with internal divisions. A projected Conservative majority was solidified shortly after 9 p.m., prompting loud cheers and sustained applause from supporters gathered at the party’s election-night headquarters at Rocky Mountaineer Station in Vancouver. An estimated 500 to 600 people attended the gathering, where supporters repeatedly erupted in applause as election results appeared on screens throughout the evening. Doerkson, 58, assumed the party’s interim leadership Sept. 20 following Kerry-Lynne Findlay’s resignation. Two days later, NDP Premier David Eby called a snap provincial election, sending British Columbians to the polls two years ahead of schedule. Doerkson is also being sent back to Victoria for the third time by the voters of the Cariboo Chilcotin. The Conservatives established leads across much of the province on Saturday, including several Metro Vancouver ridings previously held by the NDP. Doerkson was first elected to the legislature in 2020 as a BC Liberal, representing Cariboo-Chilcotin, and joined the Conservatives in 2024. Before entering provincial politics, he worked as a community newspaper publisher. His appointment as interim leader followed months of Conservative infighting, caucus departures and changes in party leadership. Following his appointment, several MLAs who had left or been expelled returned to the Conservative caucus. 150448b73a0f1e2ebf11526ab858bb91.text: B.C. Votes 2026: BC Conservative Pavneet Singh wins Kelowna-Lake Country-Coldstream riding | Williams Lake Tribune B.C. Votes 2026: BC Conservative Pavneet Singh wins Kelowna-Lake Country-Coldstream riding BC Conservative candidate Pavneet Singh arrives at the Fairfield Inn in Kelowna after winning the riding on final voting day, Oct. 24, 2026. BC Conservative candidate Pavneet Singh arrives at the Fairfield Inn in Kelowna after winning the riding on final voting day, Oct. 24, 2026. Kelowna-Lake Country-Coldstream has a new MLA, as the BC Conservatives’ Pavneet Singh has been elected. Singh beat out BC NDP candidate Binny Boparai, Green candidate Carter Mochinski and OneBC candidate Alexandra Wright to win the riding. In a brief interview with media, Singh thanked volunteers and supporters. Media, including Black Press, were barred by the Conservative campaign managers on scene from listening to Singh’s victory speech at the Fairfield Inn on Powick Road on election night on Oct. 24. Singh told media, “Today is not the time for media interviews, today is for the volunteers, family and friends who supported us.” Singh said he would be available for interview at a later date. With one ballot box left to be counted, Singh has 47.44 per cent of the vote (10,453 votes).

With a Conservative Party of BC majority government forecast, and with Conservative candidate Megan Knight projected to win the riding of Surrey South, CentreBC leader and Surrey South candidate Elenore Sturko was a little emotional as she spoke to her team at CentreBC headquarters Saturday night. The CentreBC office was filed with positive energy throughout election night, despite the party not being projected to win any seats in the provincial legislature. “I’m a bit emotional as I deliver this speech tonight, but please know it’s not because I’m sad. It’s because I’ve so enjoyed serving my community and the gravity of knowing how many of you supported me during these last four years of elected service, and now that that is changing, it’s heavy,” Sturko told her supporters, other CenterBC candidates, and volunteers after former NDP premier David Eby conceded the majority Conservative win. “Tonight the results may not be what we hoped for. We may not have won a seat in the legislature and I know it’s disappointing because we did work hard. We believed in what we were building and we wanted the opportunity to put our ideas into action. But I want you to remember something,” Sturko continued. “The value of what we have accomplished cannot be measured by the number of seats that we’ve won tonight. Just weeks ago Center BC was a party with potential but limited resources, a small team, and a long work ahead of us. Together we built something very special. We recruited candidates across British Columbia. We brought new voices into public life, developed great platforms focused on practical solutions, and took our message directly to the people,” she said. He promised to encourage investment, increase liquefied natural gas production and deliver on his campaign commitment not to introduce new taxes. Doerkson, who took over the party’s interim leadership just five weeks ago, thanked outgoing Premier David Eby for his years of public service and congratulated Green Party Leader Emily Lowan on her election victory. In Burnaby South-Metrotown, the NDP holds a 39-vote advantage, with only one ballot box outstanding in the initial count. Provincewide, Conservatives lead in 63 ridings, compared with 28 for the NDP and two for the Greens. Just over 92 per cent of ballot boxes have reported, although outstanding ballots and the final count could change the outcome of close constituency races. I really think that this community is very special and I’m hoping to be able to really make a difference here.” Acton, an entrepreneur and registered massage therapist who has lived in the riding since 1991, was voted in as Lumby’s mayor for a sixth time in last week’s local government elections. 1b4ca04c8bd0ed76c493ca7411c36478.text: Polls now closed in B.C. election, counting underway | Williams Lake Tribune A Voting Place sign outside AJ McLellan Elementary School in Surrey on Oct. 16, 2026. Polls have closed across B.C., and counting has started except in Grassy Plains, on the Southside of Francois Lake in the Nechako Lakes riding of Northwest B.C., where the polling station will remain open until 10 p.m. Elections B.C. confirmed that voters on the Southside would have the extra two hours tonight after the polls opened late this morning, after 10 a.m. Today, Oct. 24, is the final day to vote in the provincial election. British Columbians are heading to the polls to vote for MLAs in 93 ridings across the province. Polls opened at 8 a.m. and will close at 8 p.m., local time. A live blog will be updated throughout the evening with coverage from party headquarters. NDP Leader David Eby called the snap election on Sept. 22 after about a week of speculation as the B.C. Conservative Party dissolved into chaos, and Kerry-Lynne Findlay quit as party leader. Two days before the election call, Lorne Doerkson was named interim Conservative leader, unifying the party and bringing more than a dozen MLAs who had quit under Findlay back into the fold before the election was called. Five parties with incumbent MLAs are hoping to expand their seat count: the NDP, the Conservative Party, the Green Party, CentreBC and OneBC. There are also a handful of smaller parties and Independents. For a list of final voting day locations across the province, click here.

As of Oct. 24, 2026 the nearly 1,300 USW Local 7619 workers at the site are on strike. The 1,277 members of United Steelworkers (USW) Local 7619 at Teck Highland Valley Copper (HVC) near Kamloops went on strike as of Saturday (Oct. 24). The collective agreement between USW Local 7619 and HVC expired on Sept. 30. Negotiations regarding terms and conditions for a new collective agreement began on June 9, with meetings continuing throughout July, August, and September. On Oct. 8, the union broke off talks with HVC to seek a strike mandate, and union members took part in a two-day strike vote on Oct. 16 and 17. According to the bargaining committee, 944 members voted in what was described as the strongest strike vote in the history of the local. The final tally showed that 100 per cent of those who voted were in favour of serving 72-hour strike notice, which was issued at 6:30 p.m. on Tuesday, Oct. 20 after HVC provided a monetary counter and removed one concession, but left other concession requests in place. An update on Oct. 21 noted that HVC had reached out to continue bargaining. However, talks between USW and HVC on Oct. 21 and 22 failed to result in a new collective agreement. On Saturday, strike captains were organizing picket lines at the main gate of Highland Valley Copper on Highway 97C between Ashcroft and Logan Lake, where union members were being directed to go to. Drivers are advised to exercise caution through the area. In addition to proposed concessions from HVC, negotiations have centred around wages, pensions, staff shortages, and retention. ad3c8bc6b4373dd676e915dd3eeeacf4.text: Vancouver Canucks defenceman Elias Pettersson fires a shot against the Minnesota Wild during NHL action Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026 at Rogers Arena in Vancouver. Amid a steady chorus of boos, Quinn Hughes had a goal and an assist, lifting the visiting Minnesota Wild to a 4-2 win over the Vancouver Canucks in NHL action Sunday at Rogers Arena in Vancouver. Hughes, the superstar defenceman and former Canucks captain, was returning to Vancouver for the first time since being acquired by Minnesota on Dec. 12, 2025. He was loudly jeered every time he touched the puck, along with various derogatory chants during the game. A tribute video during a break seven minutes into the first period drew a mixture of cheers and boos, with Hughes acknowledging the fans with a raised stick. Maxim Shabanov, Bobby Brink and Kirill Kaprizov also scored for the Wild (8-3-2), with Calvin Pickard making 15 saves for the goaltending win. Max Sasson and Brock Boeser scored for the Canucks (2-10-1), who have dropped 10 straight games. Leevi Merilainen took the loss for Vancouver, stopping 30 of 34 shots. The Canucks came out strong, not allowing the Wild a shot for the first six minutes, but they could not beat Pickard. With 1:27 left in the period, Shabanov tapped in a no-look, cross-crease pass from Kaprizov for his third goal of the season, on a Wild power play. The Wild began to take control in the middle frame. Brink made it 2-0 at 5:54, making a slick move to fool Merilainen and scoring his first goal of the year. Seven minutes later on another Wild power play, Hughes scored his third of the year, slipping out from behind the net to knock in a rebound to the left of Merilainen. It was the 500th point of his NHL career. In the third period, Hughes sprung Kaprizov for a breakaway, and he beat Merilainen at 3:38 for his 13th of the year. 8037bcbc8635712289cdc7690574ea32.text: Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson addresses the media in Vancouver on Oct. 25, 2026, the morning after his sweeping electoral victory. Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson pitched unity and quick action in his first media appearance just 12 hours after leading the B.C. Conservative Party to a sweeping electoral victory. “To the British Columbians who voted for another party yesterday, I heard you,” he said. “Starting today, I am your premier as much as anyone else’s. You will have a government that listens to you, works for you, and respects you, however you marked your ballot.” Because he was appointed to lead his party just two days before the Sept. 22 snap election call, Doerkson is technically the interim leader. But he brushed aside the notion that he would step aside and allow for a leadership race. “I am leader, and that’s an administrative detail,” he said. “There’ll be more information on that imminently, but I will remain as leader of the party, and I’m thrilled to be the premier of British Columbia right now.” He says he will act quickly to address emergency room closures that have plagued small communities throughout B.C., promising that within his first 100 days in office he will establish a commission to work on keeping ERs open and cutting wait times. As the MLA for the Cariboo-Chilcotin riding, Doerkson knows the concerns with recurring temporary closures of emergency services, with 100 Mile House’s ER having more than 37 closures this year. Doerkson was re-elected to a third term in the riding. He also promises an independent review of the government’s finances. B.C.’s deficit is nearly $14 billion, and multiple credit rating agencies downgraded the province’s rating in recent years. “Before we table a budget, you will have the full picture,” he said. Doerkson also says he will immediately work on promised changes to election rules to avoid overlapping provincial and municipal elections. 655c8bdab7ead0583824131a37668dd8.text: 2026 B.C. election sees record low turnout as Conservatives win majority | Williams Lake Tribune 2026 B.C. election sees record low turnout as Conservatives win majority A large number of British Columbians opted out of the democratic process in the 2026 provincial election, according to preliminary results. The elections, which resulted in a landslide victory for the BC Conservatives on Oct. 24, saw the lowest turnout in the province’s history, with only 48.1 per cent of registered voters casting their ballots with 99.75 per cent of boxes reporting. The result marks an over 10 per cent decrease in voter turnout percentage compared to the 2024 provincial elections, and is nearly six per cent lower than B.C.’s second-worst voter turnout in 2020, during the COVID pandemic. As of Sunday afternoon, Oct. 25, ElectionsBC had 1,798,103 votes considered of 3,738,182 registered voters, which represents the lowest number of total votes since the 2009 election. ElectionsBC is still counting vote-by-mail ballots, assisted telephone voting ballots, absentee ballots cast at special voting opportunities and absentee ballots cast on final voting day. BC NDP Leader David Eby, and now former premier, called the election two years early in an attempt to win a majority for the party’s fourth term. The snap election was announced about a week after the governing party’s main political opponents, the BC Conservatives, lost the former leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay as she resigned. Since then, Cariboo-Chilcotin MLA Lorne Doerkson took the helm for the BC Conservatives on a technical interim basis. Speaking to reporters on Oct. 25, Doerkson said the interim label is an “administrative detail” and expects to be the leader of the party and the next Premier of B.C. We can explore the influence Karen is having on the 2025 releases, while we harken back to Adega’s founders, the Nunes and Farinha families and their earlier vintage Portuguese style red wines. Naramata Bench grown, the Adega 2025 Chardonnay is lightly oaked, dry and crisp. Hand picked and gently pressed; it highlights aromas and flavours of Okanagan stone fruits, spice and sage. Salmon coloured in the glass, it is dry well balanced and packs a ton of fresh berry and citrus aromas and flavours. The balanced acidity and tannins give it a smooth mouthfeel. NDP leader after party loses election Former premier David Eby is led off the stage by his wife Cailey Lynch after conceding the 2026 B.C. election. David Eby has conceded the 2026 B.C. election and stepped down as B.C. NDP leader. “This is obviously something I do with a heavy heart,” he told supporters gathered in downtown Vancouver on Saturday night. “But it is time for new leadership within our party.” Eby called the snap election on Sept. 22 as the opposition Conservative Party looked to be in disarray. Former Conservative leader Kerry-Lynne Findaly stepped down just two days earlier amid a caucus uprising, and the party appeared to be splitting in two. But Lorne Doerkson took the helm as interim Conservative leader, and quickly unified the ranks. He is now projected to be premier-designate after leading the party to a sweeping electoral victory. Eby is still projected to win the Vancouver-Point Grey riding, but the Conservative Party appears to have flipped nearly 20 seats. Bowinn Ma, the NDP’s candidate for North Vancouver-Lonsdale, thanked former NDP Leader David Eby for his service and backed him up for calling the snap election. “I understand why he called this election,” she said. “We were dealing with a very slim majority, which we made work, definitely, but we did so at the expense of many of our MLAs, who sacrificed their health.” Eby has said that with a one-vote majority, passing legislation was difficult. ee9c952149ec2bca262c060d44928cc5.text: Langley-Walnut Grove stays Conservative in B.C. election | Williams Lake Tribune Langley-Walnut Grove Conservative candidate Misty Van Popta applauded results that showed her party on its way to a majority government on Saturday night. Langley-Walnut Grove Conservative incumbent celebrated with her family after her second provincial electoral win on Saturday. Langley-Willowbrook NDP candidate Andrew Mercier and Langley-Walnut Grove candidate Holly Isaac were at the NDP election night event. Incumbent Conservative MLA Misty Van Popta held her riding again, and will now be heading to Victoria as part of the governing party. With all the election day ballots reporting and three of four advance ballot boxes counted, Van Popta was ahead with 7,552 votes, or 55.44 per cent of the total cast. Holly Isaac of the NDP received 4,362 votes, or 32.02 per cent. Green Party’s Sam Meyer received 1,107 votes for 8.13 per cent, and Kyle Stevenson of CentreBC took 586 votes, or 4.3 per cent. The party’s local success came as the Conservatives won a majority government. “More than Langley has spoken for that decisive change,” said Van Popta. She said she was thankful for her support, and also thanked the other candidates who had run against her for putting their names forward. “You never look at the polls, the only thing that matters is today,” she said. Once in Victoria, Van Popta said her priorities would be Langley Memorial Hospital, long-term care, and schools. “I’m obviously disappointed we didn’t get the result were looking for,” Isaac said. She said she was proud of her campaign team and extended her congratulations to Van Popta. The new riding was first contested in 2024, after boundaries were re-drawn. From 2020 to 2024, much of that region was represented by Megan Dykeman of the NDP, who was unseated by Van Popta. d85e7fd6b5e77ef2142078f7bb8d5eac.text: Macklin McCall was re-elected in the West Kelowna-Peachland riding in the 2026 provincial election. Macklin McCall has been re-elected in West Kelowna-Peachland in a landslide vote. With just two ballot boxes left to be counted, McCall has more than 62 per cent of the vote, according to the preliminary numbers. “What a humbling and exciting night, I am honoured to be re-elected as your MLA and grateful for the trust our community has placed in me once again,” McCall said in an emailed statement to Black Press Media. “This is an opportunity to get results on the priorities that matter most to residents, including healthcare, housing, infrastructure, and support for local businesses.” The BC Conservative Party has also won a majority government for the first time in nearly 100 years. “Tonight, British Columbians voted for change and chose a BC Conservative government focused on the issues that matter most: affordability, public safety, healthcare, and economic opportunity,” said McCall. In 2024, McCall won the riding with 50.9 per cent of the vote. Now, he’ll be returning to Victoria to represent West Kelowna-Peachland. “I look forward to returning to Victoria with a strong mandate to represent our community and deliver on the commitments we made during this campaign,” added McCall. “Tonight we celebrate. Tomorrow, the work begins… thank you, West Kelowna-Peachland. It is an honour to serve you.”

88ca090372f0c832534d0187a3e8ed2f.text: An attempted break-in reported on early Monday morning at Delainey's Lock & Key, a store in downtown Williams Lake. The business's security camera captured the face of one of the man trying to break in. An attempted break-in was reported early Monday morning at Delainey’s Lock & Key in Williams Lake. The incident has left Krista Storoschuk, owner of Delainey’s, facing damage to her business and renewed frustration, about 11 months after two thieves broke in and stole approximately $5,000 worth of hunting knives. Storoschuk said her security cameras recorded someone trying to force open the business’s door at approximately 5:03 a.m. on Oct. 26. Storoschuk said the footage showed someone repeatedly shouldering and kicking the door before using a hammer to pry off part of the frame. The door sustained damage, but the lock held and no one gained entry. She added that one person tilted a security camera, apparently trying to avoid being recorded, but the movement instead provided a close view of the person’s face. “No one was on the property at the time,” Storoschuk said. Although the building has an alarm, it did not activate because no one entered. After waking and reviewing the camera alerts, Storoschuk contacted RCMP at approximately 8 a.m. She said an officer attended and she provided surveillance videos and a close-up image of the person’s face. According to Storoschuk, the officer planned to consult colleagues to see whether anyone recognized the people recorded and said police will follow up with her. The incident comes approximately 11 months after a previous break-in at the business. Storoschuk said two people smashed the glass in the main entrance and entered the store. She shared, “They did gain entry to my establishment and stole about $5,000 worth of hunting knives.” She also said the police examined the scene for identifying evidence. Interior security cameras recorded the intruders, but their faces were covered. “We never found the culprits,” she added

c50bfbd6018fd15937ce3be3108dacbf.text: Cariboo-Chilcotin MLA-elect Lorne Doerkson (l) speaks with a resident in Cache Creek while on the campaign trail on Oct. 4. Doerkson led the BC Conservatives to a resounding victory on Oct. 24, and is on track to become the province's next premier, and the first from the Interior since 1986. British Columbians who didn’t stay up for the provincial election results on Saturday, Oct. 24, woke up on Sunday morning to find that the province has a new premier-in-waiting: Lorne Doerkson of the BC Conservatives, whose party swept into power for the first time since 1933. Few (if any) people still living will remember that last provincial Conservative government, but many will be asking themselves who Lorne Doerkson is. First elected provincially in the Cariboo-Chilcotin riding in 2020, as a member of the BC Liberal Party, and re-elected in 2024 as a BC Conservative, Doerkson has been extremely visible and active in his huge Interior riding — which runs from just west of Kamloops to west and north of Anahim Lake in the Chilcotin — but has largely flown under the radar during his relatively short political career. Doerkson would probably be among the first to acknowledge that his route to the premiership has been anything but typical. Of the last five B.C. premiers, three were political staffers and two were lawyers, and many MLAs start their road to the provincial legislature via local politics: the MLAs-elect for the two Kamloops ridings bordering Cariboo-Chilcotin, Peter Milobar and Ward Stamer, were first the mayors of Kamloops and Barriere respectively. Doerkson’s path was considerably different, and more colourful. Born in New Westminster in 1968, he grew up in Surrey and Salmon Arm before moving to Williams Lake in 2001. He previously sold advertising for the Salmon Arm Observer and worked as publisher for three other papers owned by David Black’s Black Press Media: the now-defunct Prince George Free Press, as well as the Williams Lake Tribune and 100 Mile Free

As the dust settles on the 2026 snap B.C. election, the Conservative Party is poised to take two-thirds of the legislative seats, and the NDP is looking for a new leader. Ravi Parmar, who eked out a third victory for the NDP in Langford-Highlands, says voters “sent a message” that the snap election was the “wrong decision.” “It was clearly a mistake. University of British Columbia political science lecturer Stewart Prest says this may go down in history as the biggest snap election blunder in Canadian history, calling it a complete “own goal” by the B.C. NDP. Slightly more than 48 per cent of British Columbians voted. Totals were down for both the Conservatives and NDP compared to 2024, with the Conservative Party recording about 50,000 fewer votes and the NDP down about 275,000, according to preliminary counts. Mario Canseco of the polling firm Research Co. says several factors could be at play, including the rainy weather. Who would bother to make and put up fake election campaign signs without a candidate’s consent? Green Party candidate in Surrey-Fleetwood, Binnema says someone put up hundreds of unauthorized signs with his name and photo last Friday (Oct. 23), a day before final voting in the B.C. election. “It’s somewhere between 100 and 200 (signs), I would say,” Binnema estimated Saturday. “It was shocking, to tell you the truth. When I turned around the corner and saw my mug (on signs), I thought, ‘Oh my goodness, how did this happen?'” The fake campaign signs feature a photo of Binnema, unlike his legitimate signs. His photo is “obviously ripped from the website,” and the signs have the wrong shade of green, he noted. “The signs say that they were authorized by my financial agent, which obviously wasn’t the case,” added Binnema, who works for an engineering company as a manager. “If you drive down 152nd (Street) near 96th (Avenue), you will notice an interesting pattern which might suggest how those signs got there,” he wrote in an email to *Surrey* *Now-Leader*. Later Saturday, Binnema clarified the situation in a phone call. “There were a whole bunch of signs that got put up last night all around Surrey and Fleetwood, including a bunch of, ‘Why a snap election? and some ‘Vote NDP out’ (signs),” Binnema said from his home in Fleetwood. “Some of my fraudulent signs were located next to those signs, so you can draw your conclusions who might have done that.” It wouldn’t take a conspiracy theorist to suggest the signs were an attempt to split the vote in Surrey-Fleetwood, where Conservative candidate Garry Purewal won with 8,691 votes over NDP incumbent Jagrup Brar (6,522 votes), followed by Binnema in third with 1,030, at last count. North Coast LNG project draws nearer to final investment decision Stephen Del Regno, Western LNG (left) at a signing ceremony for the Heads of Agreement with SEFE in May 2026. SEFE has now converted that preliminary deal into a 20-year commitment to buy one million tonnes of LNG per year. A floating LNG liquefaction facility proposed for north of Prince Rupert has now secured binding contracts for more than half its planned production. On Oct. 26, Ksi Lisims LNG announced it had converted its May 2026 heads of agreement to a binding sale and purchase agreement (SPA) with Securing Energy for Europe (SEFE), a state-owned German energy company. Under the agreement, SEFE would purchase one million tonnes of LNG per annum (mtpa) over 20 years. This brings Ksi Lisims completed binding SFAs to 7 million mtpa, or roughly 58 per cent, of the 12 million mtpa the company plans to produce once in production currently scheduled to begin in the early 2030s. It also brings the Western LNG, Rockies LNG and Nisga’a Nation partnership closer to the goal of having a final investment decision (FID) by the end of 2026. Large scale energy projects typically need at least 75 per cent of their project capacity locked into long-term deals to secure bank and institutional financing. A spokesperson for Western LNG said the company expects to have such deals signed for all 12 mtpa and an FID this year. “The project remains on track to reach full commercialization by the end of the year,” a press release stated. “Each new agreement brings Ksi Lisims LNG closer to construction, and closer to the jobs, training and long-term revenue our people have worked toward for generations,” said Eva Clayton, president of the Nisga’a Lisims Government. “As a co-developer, our Nation is proving that Canada’s resources can reach world markets in a way that respects our lands and our rights. However, the voter support, seen in the graph on the right, tells a different story of the wishes of the voters. The British Columbia provincial election on Oct. 24 gave the Conservatives a majority government, winning 64 of 93 seats in the legislature, with the New Democratic Party winning 27 seats and the BC Greens winning two. However, the voter statistics told a different story: fewer than half of voters marked their ballots for a Conservative. A total of 48.1 per cent of voters cast ballots for the Conservatives, while 37.4 per cent voted for a BC NDP candidate and 11 per cent supported a BC Green candidate. The remaining 3.5 per cent of voters supported all other parties, including OneBC and Centre BC. OneBC received support from 1.5 per cent of voters, and Centre BC had support from 1.6 per cent of voters. Under the first-past-the-post election structure in British Columbia and at the federal level, it is possible for a party to win a majority of seats despite having lower support from the voters. Fair Vote Canada has criticized the voting structure and is calling for a proportional representation system, similar to the electoral systems used in more than 80 per cent of western democracies. “In many countries with proportional representation, cooperation across the aisle is the norm and better long-term outcomes on the economy, health and the environment are the result,” the organization said in a statement. “For the sake of all BC voters, it’s time to put proportional representation back on the agenda.” Fair Vote Canada said a 2025 poll showed that 75 per cent of British Columbians would support a proportional representation system. Around two years after it was established, the encampment of unhoused individuals off Highway 97 in Penticton has been ordered to be cleared by a B.C. Justice. In her oral reasons for judgement, Justice Briana Hardwick issued an injunction barring the occupation of the road dedication that had been transformed into an impromptu fenced community of tents and temporary structures, with it coming into effect at noon on Oct. 30. The injunction requires all of the temporary structures to be cleared, and all of the residents of the encampment to vacate the area. Over more than an hour in Penticton Supreme Court, and ahead of longer written reasons that will be published later in the week, Justice Hardwick gave a shortened breakdown of her findings, in particular that ordering a single specific property to be cleared did not violate any of the residents’ rights, and that by forcing them to leave it would not increase the risks they already face as unhoused individuals. “Neither the general evidence of the social problems of homelessness, or the defendants’ sincere subjective views on the Fairview Encampments benefits demonstrate the requisite causal connection required to establish a breach of Section 7 of the Charter,” Hardwick said. “In summary, I find that the Fairview Encampment presents a significant ongoing public safety risk, the road dedication is simply unsuitable in any condition for an encampment.” Justice Hardwick noted that the ongoing risk of fires presented by the encampment were well

1292bf8ecdaafbec004ceaf3d29054ab.text: Two ferry sailings are at risk early Thursday amid Georgia Strait wind warning. BC Ferries’ CEO Nicolas Jimenez has moved on for unspecified reasons, and BC Ferries’ board says it initiated a leadership transition and launched a revitalization review. According to BC Ferries, Brian Anderson, vice president of strategy and planning, has been appointed as the interim CEO, while Dallyn Willis, executive vice president and chief financial officer, assumes responsibility for strategy and planning and leads the revitalization review with oversight from the board. “The ferry system is a lifeline for coastal residents and businesses, and critical to the province’s economy. The review will define new ways to optimize the system and improve how BC Ferries delivers services for customers and coastal communities,” noted a news release from BC Ferries. Under the Coastal Ferry Act, BC Ferries undergoes a regulatory review and contract discussions every four years to set limits on fares and establish required service levels. “The board thanks outgoing CEO Nicolas Jimenez for his contributions to BC Ferries and wishes him success in his future endeavours,” noted the release. Jimenez was appointed as CEO in March 2023. Over his tenure, he has overseen price hikes and the controversial plan for a Chinese company to build four new major hybrid-electric vessels by spring 2029. Over the provincial election, the BC NDP was under fire from the Conservatives for overloaded routes, cancelled sailings and high fares. The new majority Conservative government has floated the idea of a B.C. Ferries Charter, which would set standards for reliability, on-time performance, capacity, affordability and customer service. BC Ferries says a formal search for a permanent successor to Jimenez will follow the review.

1c293bae0bddba8d3da1d6d814cc960d.text: BC NDP candidate Stephanie Higginson has pulled ahead in the Ladysmith-Oceanside riding, after preliminary results of the provincial election were corrected. Higginson now sits at 13,380 (44.37 per cent), 13 votes ahead of Kris McNichol of the BC Conservative Party’s 13,367 votes (44.33 per cent). Charlene Smylie of the BC Green Party sits in third place with 3,365 votes (11.16 per cent). Elections BC noted Monday that results reported on election night are preliminary and subject to change as they are verified for accuracy and completeness. The results were updated last night (Oct. 25) to correct a data entry error, according to Elections BC. “A recount of the results reported on election night will take place for Ladysmith-Oceanside,” Elections BC said in an email. “There are also absentee and mail-in ballots left to count in that district.” The recount and count of absentee and mail-in ballots will take place from Nov. 6 to Nov. 10. Results will not be finalized until these counts are complete. “I think there’s still a lot of unknowns,” Higginson said. “It’s always nice to be going into a recount on the higher side of the ledger, but we have learned in this election not to take anything for granted.” Higginson added her priorities, if elected, will be to check-in with the new mayors and councils and First Nations and see what their priorities are. Preliminary election night results from Oct. 24 previously had McNichol ahead by 89 votes. McNichol said there will be a recount and every vote will be counted and noted the change was due to “a human error”. “This is democracy at its finest,” he added. “We’ll see what happens in the recount and the mail-in ballots and all those ballots.” If elected, McNichol said his first priority is to see the new cath lab built at Nanaimo Regional General Hospital.

f5eba8432acb12d1cc1b181ed2fcbd28.text: Halloween is a fun time for most people, but it can be a scary (and dangerous) time for pets and wildlife. Halloween is a fun time for many people, but it can present plenty of hazards for animals, both domestic and wild. Loud noises such as doorbells ringing, unexpected visitors and open doors, fireworks, exposure to potential toxins, and discarded candy wrappers are all things that can make animals anxious or present health threats. Here are three important tips to keep pets safe: **1) Keep the candy away from your pets:** While pets can enjoy their own treats or small portions of plain pumpkin, many human candies can be toxic to dogs and cats. A study found that more than 40 per cent of chocolate toxicity-related claims in B.C. happen between October and December. Additionally, wrappers can be a choking hazard. If you suspect your pet has ingested toxic food or is choking, contact your vet. **2) Keep your pet’s environment calm:** Halloween fireworks and doorbells can be stressful, especially for senior or anxious pets. The BC SPCA reports a spike of emergency calls on Halloween night. It is best to create a safe, secure, and quiet area for your pets. Playing classical music in the background, or having a radio or TV on, helps cover outside noises, while familiar smells and items like a blanket can provide comfort. If your pet experiences extreme anxiety from fireworks, consult your vet in advance. **3) Update your pet’s ID registry:** It is best to keep pets safe and comfortable at home. However, with the door opening frequently for trick-or-treaters, pets can slip out and run away. Permanent identification (ID) like microchips or tattoos is essential for a safe return. However, IDs are only effective if they are registered and the information is up to date. Have you moved since registering your pet, or has your contact information changed?
